> LineStorm is a low-cost autonomous robot designed to follow a predefined path using infrared sensors and motor control. This project combines robotics, electronics, CAD design, and programming to create a compact, reliable, and efficient robot. What makes it mine is the hands-on design process, careful component placement, chassis stabilization, dimension checks, and budget-conscious hardware selection.

Line-Follower Robot — Project Journal
Project Journal
This journal records my progress while designing a line-following robot. It documents the work completed, what I learned, challenges, and next steps.

Day 1 — Researching Designs
What I did
Explored different line-follower robot designs.
Compared general chassis layouts and considered how the sensors, controller, motor driver, and motors might fit together.
Researched the basic parts used in a line-following robot.
What I learned
A line follower uses sensors to detect a line on the surface.
The controller uses sensor readings to adjust the motors and steer the robot.
Chassis layout and component placement affect stability and assembly.
Problems / Challenges
I needed to compare different designs before deciding which layout would be practical to build.
Day 1 Status
Initial design research completed.

Start:- 3:00 p.m. to 7:20 p.m. Time:- 4 hrs 20 mins

Day 2 — Finalising the Design
What I did
Finalised the line-follower robot as my project.
Studied the basic working principle of the robot.
Considered how the sensors, controller, motor driver, motors, and chassis work together.
What I learned
Sensors detect whether the robot is aligned with the line.
The controller uses sensor readings to decide how the motors should move.
The robot follows the path by adjusting its direction when the sensor readings change.
Problems / Challenges
The exact components and their final placement still need to be confirmed as the design develops.
Day 2 Status
Project concept selected and basic working principle studied.

Start:- 5:00 p.m. to 8:30 p.m. Time:- 3 hrs 30 mins

Day 3 — Starting the Chassis Model in Onshape
What I did
Created an Onshape account.
Started modelling the robot chassis.
Considered where the main components should be positioned on the chassis.
What I learned
Onshape can be used to create and edit 3D part models.
Planning component placement early can help make the design easier to assemble.
Component dimensions and mounting points need to be considered while modelling the chassis.
Problems / Challenges
The chassis layout may need adjustments once the exact component dimensions are confirmed.
Day 3 Status
Onshape account created; chassis modelling and component-placement planning started.

Start:- 10:00 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. Time:- 4 hrs 30 mins

Day 4 — Building the Components
What I did
Continued building/modelling the components for the robot.
Worked on developing the mechanical layout around the chassis.
Considered how the parts will fit together.
What I learned
Component models should match the real parts as closely as possible.
Clearances and mounting positions matter when fitting components to a chassis.
The design should be checked as a whole before moving to assembly.
Problems / Challenges
Component dimensions and fit still need to be checked against the final parts.
Day 4 Status
Component modelling/building started.

Start:- 2:00 p.m. to 7:35 p.m. Time:- 5 hrs 35 mins

Day 5 — Component Placement and Chassis Checks
What I did
Worked on placing the robot components on the chassis.
Checked the planned component arrangement for stability and balance.
Reviewed chassis and component dimensions to identify possible fit or clearance issues.
Researched component specifications to help confirm dimensions, mounting requirements, and compatibility.
What I learned
Component placement affects the robot's balance, stability, and ease of assembly.
Checking dimensions before finalising the layout helps identify fit problems early.
Component specifications should be checked against the planned design rather than assumed.
Problems / Challenges
Final fit and compatibility depend on confirming the specifications of the actual components.
Day 5 Status
Component placement, stabilisation review, dimension checks, and component-specification research carried out.

Start:- 5:00 p.m. to 9:30 p.m. Time:- 4 hrs 30 mins

Day 6 — Creating the Bill of Materials (BOM)
What I did
Started preparing a Bill of Materials (BOM) for the line-follower robot.
Organised the components needed for the planned build.
Considered recording each part's name, quantity, specifications, and source or estimated cost where available.
What I learned
A BOM helps track the parts required to build the robot.
Listing quantities and specifications makes purchasing and assembly easier.
The BOM should match the final design and be updated when components change.
Problems / Challenges
Any unconfirmed component specifications, prices, or sources need to be verified before the BOM is treated as final.
Day 6 Status
BOM preparation started.

Start:- 8:50 a.m. to 12:40 p.m. Time:- 3 hrs 50 mins

Day 7 — Final Check
What I did
Reviewed the overall line-follower robot design.
Checked the planned chassis dimensions and component placement.
Reviewed stability, clearances, and component compatibility.
Checked the design and BOM for missing or inconsistent information.
What I learned
A final review can catch design issues before fabrication or assembly.
The chassis, component layout, and BOM should agree with one another.
Any unverified measurements or specifications should be confirmed before building.
Problems / Challenges
Final approval depends on resolving any outstanding dimension, fit, or component-specification checks.
Day 7 Status
Final design review completed; outstanding items should be verified before fabrication or assembly.

Next Steps
Confirm the dimensions of the actual components and their mounting points.
Resolve any remaining fit, clearance, stability, or compatibility issues.
Finalise the component placement and BOM using verified specifications.
Confirm the exact controller, IR sensors, motor driver, motors, and wiring before adapting and testing the firmware.
Start:- 6:50 p.m. to 9:15 p.m. Time:- 3 hrs 45 mins
